title: Payments slow right after release
executive_summary: INC-005 (SEV1) reported payment and order latency degradation beginning around 11:40Z, shortly after the payment-service 5.8.0 release. The validated final status is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED, with the leading hypothesis (H1, confidence 0.75) being storage/WAL degradation on the postgres volume vol-0a3f. This degradation saturated the database connection pool and caused statement timeouts that surfaced as payment and order latency and errors. The 5.8.0 release is not the trigger. The degradation began before the release: volume write latency rose from 11:21Z (logpat-postgres-d629c24d), postgres p99 latency rose from a 25 ms baseline to about 1340 ms from 11:23Z (met-postgres-p99_latency_ms-1110-1205), and connection utilisation climbed from 40% to 74% on average, peaking at 96%, from 11:26Z (met-postgres-db_conn_util_pct-1110-1205). The charges.insert and orders.update statements began exceeding the 2000 ms timeout at 11:28Z (logpat-payment-service-c828e437, logpat-order-service-22402aae). Payment-service p95 latency stepped up at 11:27Z (met-payment-service-p95_latency_ms-1110-1205). The 5.8.0 deployment at 11:32Z (dep-31448d11) came after all of these signals and was rejected as the cause (H2). The report_rollup batch (H3) was also rejected as the origin, because it started after the storage degradation.

hypotheses.description: Storage/WAL degradation on postgres volume vol-0a3f saturated the database connection pool, causing statement timeouts that surface as payment and order latency and errors. This is the leading explanation; the 5.8.0 release is not the trigger. Mechanism: vol-0a3f write latency degrades (avg 835 ms) from 11:21Z -> WAL writes and checkpoints slow (453-497 s) from 11:24Z -> postgres p99 latency rises from 25 ms to ~1340 ms (onset 11:23Z) and connection utilisation climbs from 40% to 74-96% (onset 11:26Z) -> charges.insert and orders.update exceed the 2000 ms statement timeout (first 11:28Z) -> payment-service p95 and error rate and order-service p95 step up (11:27-11:28Z) -> customer-visible slowness and failures after T0.

critic_review.summary: H1 (storage/WAL degradation on postgres vol-0a3f exhausting DB connections and causing statement timeouts) is the best-supported explanation and is consistent in time. Independent sources agree on an 11:21-11:23Z onset: storage write-latency logs (11:21:06Z), postgres disk_io_wait (onset 11:22Z, ~65x rise), postgres p95/p99 latency (onset 11:23Z), WAL-slow checkpoint logs (11:24Z), then connection utilisation (11:26Z), then charges.insert/orders.update timeouts (11:28Z), then payment p95 (11:27Z) and error rate (11:28Z). Postgres CPU fell, so the pressure is I/O and connections rather than compute. Redis and auth are flat. H2 is rejected: payment p95 and error rate step up at 11:27-11:28Z, before the 11:32Z 5.8.0 deployment, and the database degradation started at 11:21-11:23Z. No config changes occurred in the window. Payment CPU and request rate are unchanged. H3 is rejected as the origin: report_rollup starts at 11:28Z, after the storage and WAL degradation. It may be a secondary contributor to connection pressure, but it cannot be the root cause. Limitations: payment p99 and timeout rate stayed flat, so the impact appears only in the p95 tail and is not fully explained. Per-route or per-instance breakdowns were not available, and the root trigger of the volume degradation is out of scope.

assessments.reasoning: Storage degradation on postgres precedes every downstream anomaly. disk_io_wait, p95/p99 latency, WAL logs, and connection utilisation all show onset at 11:21-11:26Z, before payment and order timeouts at 11:27-11:28Z. The mechanism is consistent with CPU falling and redis/auth being flat. The tail-only payment p99 pattern is a residual inconsistency, not a contradiction of timing.

Payment p95 onset is 11:27Z and error-rate onset is 11:28Z, both before the 11:32Z deployment. Database anomalies start at 11:21-11:23Z. Payment CPU and request rate are unchanged. No config changes in the window. The deployment cannot be the cause of effects that precede it.

report_rollup starts at 11:28Z, after storage (11:21Z), disk I/O wait (11:22Z), and WAL (11:24Z) degradation. It is at most a secondary contributor to connection pressure. It does not explain the origin of the anomaly.

probable_root_cause.description: Storage/WAL degradation on postgres volume vol-0a3f saturated the database connection pool, causing statement timeouts that surface as payment and order latency and errors. This is the leading explanation; the 5.8.0 release is not the trigger.

root_cause_statement: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence): infrastructure_degradation in postgres - Storage/WAL degradation on postgres volume vol-0a3f saturated the database connection pool, causing statement timeouts that surface as payment and order latency and errors. This is the leading explanation; the 5.8.0 release is not the trigger.
corrective_actions: Mitigate the degraded postgres volume vol-0a3f: fail over or move the database to healthy storage, or otherwise restore write latency, and confirm that WAL write and checkpoint times return to baseline (logpat-postgres-7ce84fae).

Reduce connection pressure while storage recovers: temporarily lower or cap application connection pools in payment-service and order-service, and shed or throttle non-critical load so that connection utilisation drops below the saturation level (met-postgres-db_conn_util_pct-1110-1205).
Pause or defer the report_rollup() batch workload until the database is stable, since it may add I/O and connection contention (logpat-postgres-44883ca5).

Do not roll back payment-service 5.8.0 on the basis of this incident alone, because the evidence does not support it as the cause (H2 rejected). Keep the rollback option open if payment errors persist after the database recovers.
preventive_actions: Investigate the root trigger of the vol-0a3f write-latency degradation with the storage or infrastructure owner. This is outside the scope of this investigation.
Add capacity and I/O headroom planning for the postgres volume, and set up a runbook for storage degradation that covers failover and connection-pool limits.
Schedule heavy batch jobs such as report_rollup() away from peak traffic, or run them on a replica, so they cannot contend with the transactional workload on the primary.

Review statement timeout and connection pool settings for charges.insert and orders.update so that database slowness fails fast and in a controlled way rather than cascading into payment and order errors.
monitoring_recommendations: Alert on postgres volume write latency (vol-0a3f avg write latency above baseline, currently about 835 ms during the incident) and on disk I/O wait, with a page on sustained deviation.
Alert on postgres p99 latency above roughly 200 ms for more than a few minutes, and on db_conn_util_pct above 80%, to detect saturation before statement timeouts begin.
Alert on WAL write and checkpoint duration (for example, checkpoints longer than 60 s) using the existing 'WAL write slow' log pattern.
Alert on statement timeout counts for charges.insert and orders.update, and on payment-service and order-service p95 latency, so that timeouts are tracked against the database signals.

Restore the per-service metric queries for payment-service and order-service. The current query for 7 metrics exceeded the 6-metric limit, so those services' p95, error, timeout, request, CPU and memory breakdowns are missing. Split the queries to get complete coverage.
Track per-route and per-instance payment p95 and error rates, to test whether the p95-only tail effect comes from a subset of routes or instances.
limitations: Payment p99 latency and timeout rate stayed flat, so the impact appears only in the p95 tail, and this is not fully explained by the database timeouts.
Per-route and per-instance breakdowns were not available, so the payment p95 tail cannot be attributed to specific routes or instances.
Metric queries for order-service and payment-service failed because they requested 7 metrics, which exceeds the 6-metric limit. Their full metric coverage is therefore missing.
The root trigger of the vol-0a3f write-latency degradation was not investigated and is out of scope.
The 5.8.0 deployment was not separately tested per pod, so a small effect after 11:32Z cannot be fully excluded.

conclusion: The validated result is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED, with storage/WAL degradation on postgres volume vol-0a3f as the leading root cause (confidence 0.75). It saturated database connections and caused statement timeouts that drove payment and order latency and errors. The timing shows the degradation started before the 5.8.0 release, so the release is not the trigger (H2 rejected), and report_rollup is not the origin (H3 rejected), although it may add connection pressure. Some limits remain. Payment p99 and timeout rate stayed flat, so the impact appears mainly in the p95 tail. Per-route and per-instance breakdowns were unavailable, and the metric queries for payment-service and order-service failed. The trigger of the storage degradation is outside this investigation's scope.
